english: worry; concern; something on your mind
usage: I have something on my mind
고민 + 이 있어요; the worry 'exists,' so use 있다, not 해요
I have a lot on my mind
많다 = to be many; the default way to say you are stressed about several things
to mull over; to agonize over a choice
고민 + 하다 turns the noun into a verb of active deliberation
warm, caring way to check on a friend who looks down
examples: 요즘 고민이 많아요.
I have a lot on my mind these days.
요즘 + 고민이 많다 is an extremely common everyday complaint
친구한테 고민을 털어놨어요.
I poured out my worries to a friend.
털어놓다 = to unload feelings; 한테 marks the person you confide in
어느 회사에 갈지 고민하고 있어요.
I'm agonizing over which company to join.
real decision context: -ㄹ지 고민하다 = wrestle with a choice
nuance: 고민 (苦悶, 苦 'bitter/suffering' + 悶 'anguish') is a problem you keep turning over in your head, usually a personal dilemma or decision you cannot resolve. The dividing line from 걱정 matters: 걱정 is anxious worry about a bad outcome you cannot control ('I'm worried it'll rain'), while 고민 is active mental wrestling over a choice you must make ('I'm torn over which job to take'). Register is neutral and everyday; you say 고민이 있어요 to a friend or 고민입니다 in a formal email. It habitually pairs with 많다, 깊다 (deep), 털어놓다 (unload), and 들어주다 (listen to someone's). The English-speaker trap: 고민 is a noun, so 'I worry' is 고민이 있어요 or 고민해요, never the non-word 고민다; and do not reach for 걱정 every time you would say 'worry' in English, because a decision dilemma is 고민, not 걱정.

Don't use 걱정 for a choice you're weighing. 'I'm torn over which one' is 고민이에요, not 걱정이에요 — 걱정 is dread about an outcome, 고민 is deliberation.
Don't translate 'have a worry' as 고민을 가지고 있어요. Korean prefers existence: 고민이 있어요.

usage: the topic ALWAYS takes 에, never 을/를
없다 = to not have; flat, common way to decline
here 관심 IS the object, so it takes 을 — the rare case 를 is correct
please pay attention / show you care
asking for caring attention, not romantic interest
examples: 저는 한국 음식에 관심이 있어요.
I'm interested in Korean food.
에 marks the thing you're interested in — lock this particle in
그 영화에는 별로 관심이 없어요.
I'm not really interested in that movie.
별로 ... 없다 = not particularly; softens the refusal
요즘 환경 문제에 관심을 가지게 됐어요.
Lately I've come to care about environmental issues.
관심을 가지게 되다 = to grow interested over time
nuance: 관심 (關心, 關 'connect/concern' + 心 'heart') is interest or attention directed toward something or someone — your heart 'connecting' to a topic. The nearest rival is 흥미: 흥미 is the fun, curious spark you get from a hobby or story ('this novel is 흥미롭다'), while 관심 is broader, covering both intellectual interest and caring, watchful attention toward a person. Register is neutral. Watch the two-faced particle behavior, which is the classic English-speaker pitfall: with 있다/없다/많다 the topic takes 에 (음악에 관심이 있어요), but with the verb 가지다 the word 관심 itself becomes the object and takes 을 (관심을 가지다). Saying 음악을 관심이 있어요 is the single most common error. Also note 관심 toward a person can imply romantic interest, so 그 사람한테 관심 있어요 often means 'I like them' — choose your words around people carefully.

Don't say 관심해요 as if it were a verb. Use 관심이 있어요 or the verb 관심을 가지다.
Be careful saying 사람한테 관심 있어요 — toward a person it usually sounds like a romantic confession, not neutral interest.

usage: 필요하다 = to be needed; the most natural frame for abstract 인내
인내 + 심(心) 'heart'; the everyday word for someone's patience
강하다 = strong; the natural collocation, not 많다
기르다 = to cultivate; patience as something you train
examples: 한국어 공부에는 인내가 필요해요.
Studying Korean takes patience.
X에는 인내가 필요하다 = X requires patience
저는 인내심이 좀 부족한 편이에요.
I'm a bit on the impatient side.
-는 편이다 = tend to be; softer than a flat statement
끝까지 참고 인내한 결과 성공했어요.
By enduring to the end, I succeeded.
참다 + 인내하다 stacked for emphasis on perseverance
nuance: 인내 (忍耐, 忍 'endure' + 耐 'bear/withstand') is the abstract virtue of patient endurance, the capacity to bear hardship without giving up. It is weighty and somewhat literary, the language of mottos, self-help, and graduation speeches. Three relatives sort out by everyday-ness: bare 인내 is the abstract concept; 인내심 (adding 心 'heart') is patience as a person's character trait and is what you use to describe someone; and 참다 is the plain native verb 'to put up with / hold back' you actually use in daily life ('I held back my anger' = 화를 참았어요). The English-speaker pitfall: don't say 인내가 많아요 to mean 'I'm patient' — patience as a trait is 인내심이 많다/강하다, and for ordinary 'be patient / hang in there' Koreans say 참아요 or 참으세요, reserving 인내하다 for serious perseverance.

mistakes: Don't describe a person with bare 인내. Patience as a trait is 인내심: 인내심이 강해요, not 인내가 강해요.
For everyday 'put up with it / be patient,' use 참다 (참으세요), not the heavy 인내하다.
Make the verb with 하다: 인내하다, never 인내다.

usage: the skill area takes 에; 자신 'exists,' so use 있다
없다 = to lack; the everyday way to admit self-doubt
자신 + 감(感) 'feeling'; the buoyant emotional state
생기다 = to arise; confidence as something that grows in you
examples: 저는 요리에 자신이 있어요.
I'm confident about cooking.
에 marks the area you're sure you can do well
이번 시험은 솔직히 자신이 없어요.
Honestly, I'm not confident about this exam.
솔직히 = honestly; natural hedge before admitting doubt
발표를 잘 끝내고 나니 자신감이 생겼어요.
After finishing the presentation well, I gained confidence.
-고 나니 = after doing, I found that...; the 자신감 'feeling' word fits here
nuance: 자신 (自身, 自 'self' + 身 'body') literally means 'one's own self,' and in 자신이 있다/없다 it has come to mean confidence in your own ability. Distinguish the two close forms: 자신이 있다 is being sure you CAN do a specific thing ('I'm confident about the test'), task-focused, while 자신감 (adding 感 'feeling') names confidence as an inner emotional state you carry around ('she radiates confidence'). The plain meaning 'oneself' survives in 자기 자신 (one's very own self) and reflexive uses. Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfalls: the area of confidence takes 에 (운동에 자신이 있어요), not 을/를; and don't translate 'I am confident' as 자신이에요 — 자신 is a noun, so it's 자신이 있어요. Beginners also confuse 자신 with 자신감; if you can replace it with 'a feeling of confidence,' use 자신감.

usage: 행복 + 하다 = the adjective; this is how you SAY you're happy
polite present of 행복하다; 하다 → 해요
느끼다 = to feel; treats 행복 as an emotion you sense
행복한 가정 (happy home), 행복한 하루 (happy day) — the modifier form
examples: 지금 정말 행복해요.
I'm really happy right now.
adjective 행복하다 → 행복해요; no 이에요 needed
작은 일에서도 행복을 느껴요.
I find happiness even in small things.
에서(도) marks where the feeling comes from; 도 = even
행복한 하루 보내세요!
Have a happy day!
행복한 + noun is a warm everyday send-off
nuance: 행복 (幸福, 幸 'good fortune' + 福 'blessing') is happiness as a deep, lasting state of well-being and contentment with one's life — bigger and more enduring than a passing good mood. Contrast it sharply with 기쁨/기쁘다 and with 기분이 좋다: 기쁘다 is the bright spike of joy from a specific event ('I'm glad I passed!'), whereas 행복하다 is the settled background sense that life is good. So winning a prize makes you 기쁘다 in the moment, but a loving family makes you 행복하다 over years. Register is warm and neutral, common in wishes like 행복하세요 and 행복한 하루. The core English-speaker pitfall: 행복 is a noun, so 'I'm happy' is the ADJECTIVE 행복해요, never 행복이에요 (which would oddly mean 'it is happiness'). Also resist using 행복하다 for momentary delight — for 'I'm so glad / happy about this news,' 기뻐요 is the natural choice.

Don't use 행복하다 for momentary delight over one event. That's 기쁘다 (기뻐요); 행복하다 is lasting well-being.
Don't add an object marker to the adjective. 'I'm happy' is just 행복해요, not 행복을 해요.

usage: 불안 + 하다 = the adjective; the everyday way to express it
느끼다 = to feel; treats 불안 as a sensed emotion
마음이 불안하다 is a fixed, very natural phrase
examples: 시험 전에는 늘 마음이 불안해요.
Before a test I always feel uneasy.
전에 = before; 늘 = always — a routine state
혼자 밤길을 걸으면 좀 불안해요.
Walking alone at night, I feel a little anxious.
everyday situation; 좀 softens it to 'a bit'
그 소식을 듣고 막연한 불안을 느꼈어요.
After that news I felt a vague unease.
막연한 불안 = vague, formless anxiety — a natural pairing
nuance: 불안 (不安, 不 'not' + 安 'peace/safe') literally means 'not at peace' — an unsettled, restless anxiety, the felt opposite of 안심 (relief/security). Separate it from 걱정: 걱정 is worry pointed at a specific thing you can name ('I'm worried about the rent'), often with a thought you could voice, while 불안 is a more diffuse, bodily sense of dread that may have no clear object ('I just feel uneasy'). 불안 is heavier and more clinical-leaning — 불안 장애 is 'anxiety disorder.' Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: 불안 is a noun, so 'I'm anxious' is the adjective 불안해요, not 불안이에요; and don't default to 걱정 for every English 'anxious,' because a free-floating jittery feeling is 불안하다, whereas fretting over a known problem is 걱정하다. The set phrase 마음이 불안하다 is your reliable way to say your heart won't settle.

Don't omit 마음이 in the idiom. 'My heart is uneasy' is 마음이 불안해요, a set collocation.

usage: 기대 + 되다; the THING takes 이/가, not 을/를 — key pattern
기대 + 하다 is the active verb and takes 을/를
크다 = big; the natural collocation, not 높다
부응하다 = to meet; formal but very common set phrase
examples: 내일 여행이 너무 기대돼요!
I can't wait for tomorrow's trip!
기대되다 with 이/가; the excited, can't-wait sense
새 영화를 정말 기대하고 있어요.
I'm really looking forward to the new movie.
기대하고 있다 = actively anticipating; here it takes 를
기대가 너무 크면 실망하기 쉬워요.
If your expectations are too high, it's easy to be let down.
기대가 크다 + 실망하다 — the natural pairing of hope and letdown
nuance: 기대 (期待, 期 'appointed time/expect' + 待 'wait') is the forward-leaning feeling of waiting for something good, or the hopes you place on a person. The 되다/하다 split is the heart of this word: 기대되다 is the involuntary 'it makes me excited / I can't wait,' so the source takes 이/가 (여행이 기대돼요); 기대하다 is the active 'I expect/anticipate it,' which takes 을/를 (여행을 기대해요). A near-synonym is 설레다 (to flutter with excitement) — but 설레다 is purely the heart-fluttering emotion, while 기대 also carries cognitive expectation about an outcome ('high expectations'). Register is neutral. The big English-speaker pitfall: by analogy with English 'I look forward to it,' learners say 여행을 기대돼요 — but 되다 is intransitive, so it must be 여행이 기대돼요. Also, 기대 cuts both ways: 기대가 크다 sets you up for 실망 (disappointment), a pairing Koreans use constantly.

Say 기대가 크다 for high expectations, not 기대가 높다 — 크다 is the standard collocation.

usage: 자유 + 롭다 = adjective; ㅂ-irregular, so 자유로워요
자유롭다 conjugates with ㅂ-irregular: 롭다 → 로워요
자유 + 시간 written as two words; super useful daily phrase
N의 자유 = the freedom to/of N; common in serious topics
examples: 주말에는 자유 시간이 많아요.
I have a lot of free time on weekends.
자유 시간 as a fixed two-word noun
혼자 여행하니까 정말 자유로워요.
Traveling alone, I feel so free.
자유롭다 → 자유로워요 (ㅂ-irregular in action)
모든 사람에게는 표현의 자유가 있어요.
Everyone has freedom of expression.
N의 자유 in the abstract civic sense
nuance: 자유 (自由, 自 'self' + 由 'follow from / on one's own') means freedom — both the grand civic idea (자유와 평등, freedom and equality) and the everyday feeling of doing as you please. The adjective 자유롭다 describes a person or situation as unconstrained; a near rival is 편하다, but 편하다 is comfort/ease ('this chair is comfy'), whereas 자유롭다 is specifically the absence of restriction or obligation ('I'm free to do what I want'). Register is neutral. Two English-speaker pitfalls. First, the adjective is 자유롭다, NOT 자유하다 — and because 롭다 follows the ㅂ-irregular pattern, the polite form is 자유로워요, not the regular-looking 자유롭어요. Second, 자유 시간 is conventionally written as two separate words; learners often jam it together as 자유시간. To say someone simply 'is free / available,' note Koreans often say 시간이 있어요 (have time) rather than forcing 자유 in.

Don't overuse 자유 for 'I'm free this weekend.' That's usually 시간 있어요; 자유 is freedom/liberty, not mere availability.

english: greed; desire to have more; ambition
usage: to feel a craving (to have it)
나다 = to arise; the urge wells up in you — use 나다, not 하다
많다 = many; describes a person's greedy character
부리다 = to act out (a trait); fixed idiom for greedy behavior
to go for more; to set one's sights high
내다 = to put forth; can be positive drive or negative grabbing
examples: 저 가방을 보니까 욕심이 나요.
Seeing that bag, I really want it.
보니까 ... 욕심이 나다 = the sight triggers the craving
그 사람은 욕심이 너무 많아요.
That person is way too greedy.
욕심이 많다 paints a character flaw
너무 욕심부리지 말고 하나만 골라요.
Don't be greedy — just pick one.

usage: 정성 + 껏 'to the fullest'; an adverb already — don't add 하게
to put in one's whole heart
다하다 = to do fully; the standard set phrase
to be filled with heartfelt care
담기다 = to be contained; said of gifts, food, letters
정성 + 스럽다 = the adjective describing caring effort
examples: 엄마가 정성껏 밥을 차려 주셨어요.
Mom lovingly prepared a meal for me.
정성껏 + 차리다; 주셨어요 honors mom doing it for me
이 선물에는 정성이 가득 담겨 있어요.
This gift is full of heartfelt care.
정성이 담기다, intensified with 가득 (brimming)
정성을 다해 손님을 대접했어요.
I served the guests with all my heart.
정성을 다하다 + 대접하다 — the language of hospitality
nuance: 정성 (精誠, 精 'refined/pure' + 誠 'sincerity') is the warm, painstaking care and sincerity you pour into doing something for someone — cooking a meal, choosing a gift, writing by hand. Koreans prize 정성 deeply: a humble homemade dish made 정성껏 outranks an expensive store-bought one. Register is warm and slightly elevated, common in thanks and hospitality. The English-speaker pitfall: 정성껏 is already a complete adverb (= 'with full sincerity'), so don't tack on 하게 to make 정성껏하게 — just say 정성껏 요리하다. Also, you GIVE 정성 to others; don't use it for cold, goal-driven effort, which is 노력.

usage: 되다 = to become; the THING that comforts takes 이/가
위로 + 하다; the person you console takes 을/를
받다 = to receive; you receive comfort from someone
의 links the nouns; said at funerals and hard times
examples: 친구의 말 한마디가 큰 위로가 됐어요.
A single word from my friend was a big comfort.
말 한마디 + 위로가 되다; the thing comforts → 이/가
힘들어하는 친구를 위로해 줬어요.
I comforted my struggling friend.
위로하다 takes the person as object; 줬어요 = did it for them
따뜻한 차 한 잔이 큰 위로가 돼요.
A warm cup of tea is a great comfort.
even an object can 위로가 되다 — 'be comforting'
nuance: 위로 (慰勞, 慰 'console/soothe' + 勞 'toil/weariness') is comfort given to someone who is sad, grieving, or worn out — soothing their hardship. A near relative is 격려 (激勵, encouragement): 격려 cheers you ON toward a future effort ('you can do it, keep going!'), while 위로 soothes present pain and sorrow ('I'm so sorry, it must be hard'). So you 격려 someone before an exam but 위로 them after a loss. Register is gentle and caring. The central English-speaker pitfall is the 되다/하다 split tied to who does what: 위로가 되다 means something IS a comfort, with the comforting thing as subject (네 말이 위로가 됐어 = 'your words comforted me'); 위로하다 means a person actively comforts ANOTHER person, who takes 을/를 (친구를 위로했어요). Saying 위로해요 when you mean 'it comforts me' is wrong — that says 'I comfort someone.' To receive comfort, use 위로를 받다.

usage: to show off / boast about N
를 marks the thing flaunted; can sound braggy
자랑 + 스럽다 = adjective; purely positive, warm pride
자랑 + 거리 'material'; a source of pride
to be the pride of N
그 학교의 자랑 = the pride of that school
examples: 친구가 새 차를 자랑했어요.
My friend showed off a new car.
자랑하다 takes 를; here it leans 'bragging'
저는 우리 가족이 정말 자랑스러워요.
I'm really proud of my family.
자랑스럽다 = warm pride; the source takes 이/가
그 선수는 온 나라의 자랑이에요.
That athlete is the pride of the whole nation.
N의 자랑이다 = to be the pride of N
nuance: 자랑 (native Korean, not Sino-Korean) covers a spectrum from honest pride to boastful showing-off, and context decides the tone. The verb 자랑하다 usually leans negative — 'to brag, to flaunt' — so calling someone's talk 자랑 hints they're full of themselves. By contrast, the adjective 자랑스럽다 is purely warm and positive: 'proud of' (아들이 자랑스러워요). Keep this split from 뽐내다 (to flaunt/preen), which is even more openly show-offy and vain. Register is neutral, though 자랑하다 can sting. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'I'm proud of you' tempts learners to build it from 자랑하다, but 자랑하다 means 'brag,' so 'I'm proud of you' must use the adjective 자랑스러워요 (or 네가 자랑스러워). With 자랑스럽다 the object of pride takes 이/가 (가족이 자랑스러워요), not 을/를; only the verb 자랑하다 (to show off) takes 을/를 (사진을 자랑하다).

usage: 의 links the nouns; inner calm
지키다 = to guard; the civic-scale collocation
examples: 시골은 정말 평화로워요.
The countryside is so peaceful.
평화롭다 → 평화로워요 (ㅂ-irregular)
명상을 하면 마음의 평화를 얻어요.
Meditating brings me peace of mind.
마음의 평화 + 얻다 (to gain) — inner calm
온 세계가 평화를 바라요.
The whole world hopes for peace.
평화를 바라다 = to wish for peace, the large-scale sense

Second, beginners eye-confuse 평화 (peace) with 평소 (平素, 'usual times / ordinarily') because both start with 평 — keep them apart: 평소에 운동해요 means 'I usually exercise,' nothing to do with peace.
